notes.front: Under the Section 608 rules, what does it mean to recover refrigerant?
notes.back: To remove refrigerant from an appliance and store it in an external container, without necessarily testing or processing it.
notes.explanation: Nothing has to be done to the refrigerant itself: getting it out and into a separate container is the whole of the step.
notes.example: Like draining a fuel tank into a can before a repair: nothing is cleaned or tested, it is only removed and kept.
notes.source: EPA, Recovering, Recycling, and Reclaiming of Refrigerants
notes.evidence: Recover means to remove refrigerant in any condition from an appliance and to store it in an external container without necessarily testing or processing it in any way
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Under the Section 608 rules, what does it mean to recycle refrigerant?
notes.back: To extract it from an appliance and clean it for reuse in equipment of the same owner, without meeting all the requirements for reclamation.
notes.explanation: Recycling goes further than recovery, since the refrigerant is cleaned, but stops short of reclamation and stays with the same owner.
notes.example: Like filtering used cooking oil to use again in your own kitchen, rather than refining it to a standard for sale.
notes.source: EPA, Recovering, Recycling, and Reclaiming of Refrigerants
notes.evidence: Recycle, when referring to refrigerant, means to extract refrigerant from an appliance (except MVACs) and clean it for reuse in equipment of the same owner without meeting all of the requirements for reclamation.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Under the Section 608 rules, what does it mean to reclaim refrigerant?
notes.back: To reprocess recovered refrigerant to the specifications in appendix A (based on AHRI Standard 700-2016) and verify it meets them.
notes.explanation: The definition has two parts: reprocessing to the specifications, and checking the result with the analytical method the appendix prescribes.
notes.example: Like refining used oil to a published grade and then proving the grade by laboratory test.
notes.source: EPA, Recovering, Recycling, and Reclaiming of Refrigerants
notes.evidence: Reclaim means to reprocess recovered refrigerant to all of the specifications in appendix A of this subpart (based on AHRI Standard 700–2016, Specifications for Refrigerants) that are applicable to that refrigerant and to verify that the refrigerant meets these specifications using the analytical methodology prescribed in section 5 of appendix A of this subpart.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: In the Section 608 test topics, what is dehydration evacuation?
notes.back: Evacuating a system at the end of service to eliminate air and moisture.
notes.explanation: The test topics give it its own heading in the core section, separate from recovery techniques.
notes.example: Like pumping the air and damp out of a storage jar before sealing it.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Dehydration Evacuation”
notes.evidence: Dehydration Evacuation - Need to evacuate system to eliminate air and moisture at the end of service

notes.front: In the refrigerant rules, what is a pump-out unit?
notes.back: System-dependent recovery equipment that is permanently attached to an appliance.
notes.explanation: The rule names it as the exception to its ban on using system-dependent equipment with appliances holding more than 15 pounds of refrigerant.
notes.example: Like a bilge pump built into a boat, rather than a portable pump brought aboard for each job.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F, § 82.156(e)
notes.evidence: System-dependent equipment may not be used with appliances with a full charge of more than 15 pounds of refrigerant, unless the system-dependent equipment is permanently attached to the appliance as a pump-out unit.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: In the refrigerant rules, what is a low-loss fitting?
notes.back: A connecting device for hoses, appliances or recovery machines that closes, automatically or by hand, when disconnected, minimising refrigerant release.
notes.explanation: The definition covers connections between hoses, appliances and recovery or recycling machines, and allows either automatic or manual closing.
notes.example: Like a garden-hose connector that shuts off the water the moment it is unplugged.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F, § 82.152 Definitions
notes.evidence: Low-loss fitting means any device that is intended to establish a connection between hoses, appliances, or recovery and/or recycling machines and that is designed to close automatically or to be closed manually when disconnected, minimizing the release of refrigerant from hoses, appliances, and recovery and/or recycling machines.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: To recover refrigerant, you remove it in {{c1::any condition}} from an appliance and store it in an external container.
notes.back: any condition
notes.explanation: Recovery need not involve any testing or processing, so the refrigerant’s state is no bar to recovering it.
notes.source: EPA, Recovering, Recycling, and Reclaiming of Refrigerants
notes.evidence: Recover means to remove refrigerant in any condition from an appliance and to store it in an external container without necessarily testing or processing it in any way
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Whose equipment may recycled refrigerant be reused in?
notes.back: Equipment of the same owner.
notes.explanation: The definition ties recycling to the same owner and says it need not meet all of the requirements for reclamation.
notes.source: EPA, Recovering, Recycling, and Reclaiming of Refrigerants
notes.evidence: Recycle, when referring to refrigerant, means to extract refrigerant from an appliance (except MVACs) and clean it for reuse in equipment of the same owner without meeting all of the requirements for reclamation.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: In general, how is recycled refrigerant cleaned?
notes.back: By oil separation and one or more passes through devices such as replaceable core filter-driers.
notes.explanation: The rule says “in general”: this is the usual method, and the filter-driers reduce moisture, acidity and particulate matter.
notes.source: EPA, Recovering, Recycling, and Reclaiming of Refrigerants
notes.evidence: In general, recycled refrigerant is cleaned using oil separation and single or multiple passes through devices, such as replaceable core filter-driers, which reduce moisture, acidity, and particulate matter.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Besides reprocessing refrigerant to the specifications, what else does reclaiming require?
notes.back: Verifying that it meets them, using the analytical method in section 5 of appendix A.
notes.explanation: Reprocessing alone is not reclamation: the definition makes testing against the standard part of the process.
notes.source: EPA, Recovering, Recycling, and Reclaiming of Refrigerants
notes.evidence: Reclaim means to reprocess recovered refrigerant to all of the specifications in appendix A of this subpart (based on AHRI Standard 700–2016, Specifications for Refrigerants) that are applicable to that refrigerant and to verify that the refrigerant meets these specifications using the analytical methodology prescribed in section 5 of appendix A of this subpart.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A technician draws refrigerant from a unit into a separate container and does nothing else to it. Recover, recycle or reclaim?
notes.back: Recover.
notes.explanation: Removing refrigerant and storing it in an external container, with no testing or processing, is exactly the definition of recovering.
notes.source: EPA, Recovering, Recycling, and Reclaiming of Refrigerants
notes.evidence: Recover means to remove refrigerant in any condition from an appliance and to store it in an external container without necessarily testing or processing it in any way
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Refrigerant is put through oil separation and filter-driers, then charged into another unit belonging to the same owner. Recover, recycle or reclaim?
notes.back: Recycle.
notes.explanation: It is cleaned for reuse in the same owner’s equipment, without the purity testing that reclamation needs.
notes.source: EPA, Recovering, Recycling, and Reclaiming of Refrigerants
notes.evidence: Recycle, when referring to refrigerant, means to extract refrigerant from an appliance (except MVACs) and clean it for reuse in equipment of the same owner without meeting all of the requirements for reclamation.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Used refrigerant is reprocessed to the AHRI Standard 700-2016 specifications and a laboratory confirms it meets them. Recover, recycle or reclaim?
notes.back: Reclaim.
notes.explanation: Reprocessing to the appendix A specifications and verifying the result by the prescribed analysis are the two parts of reclaiming.
notes.source: EPA, Recovering, Recycling, and Reclaiming of Refrigerants
notes.evidence: Reclaim means to reprocess recovered refrigerant to all of the specifications in appendix A of this subpart (based on AHRI Standard 700–2016, Specifications for Refrigerants) that are applicable to that refrigerant and to verify that the refrigerant meets these specifications using the analytical methodology prescribed in section 5 of appendix A of this subpart.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: May recovered refrigerant go back into the appliance it came from, or another appliance of the same owner, without being recycled or reclaimed?
notes.back: Yes, unless the appliance is an MVAC or an MVAC-like appliance.
notes.explanation: The rule allows this return “without being recycled or reclaimed”, and carves out only motor vehicle air conditioners and MVAC-like appliances.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F, § 82.156(h)
notes.evidence: (h) Refrigerant may be returned to the appliance from which it is recovered or to another appliance owned by the same person without being recycled or reclaimed, unless the appliance is an MVAC or MVAC-like appliance.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A supermarket chain’s technician recovers refrigerant from a system in one of its stores and wants to charge it into a system at another store the chain owns. Must it be reclaimed first?
notes.back: No. It may go into another appliance owned by the same person without being recycled or reclaimed.
notes.choices:
A) No: it may go into another appliance of the same owner
B) Yes: all recovered refrigerant must be reclaimed
C) Yes, unless it is first sold to the chain
notes.choicesExplained: B: the rule lets recovered refrigerant return to the same owner’s appliances without reclaiming. C: the chain already owns it; a sale to a new owner is what triggers reclamation.
notes.explanation: Both systems belong to the same owner, and neither is a motor vehicle air conditioner, so the same-owner rule applies.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F, § 82.156(h)
notes.evidence: (h) Refrigerant may be returned to the appliance from which it is recovered or to another appliance owned by the same person without being recycled or reclaimed, unless the appliance is an MVAC or MVAC-like appliance.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Before used refrigerant can be sold to a new owner, what must happen to it?
notes.back: It must be reclaimed by a refrigerant reclaimer certified by the Environmental Protection Agency.
notes.explanation: The regulations restrict resale to a new owner unless the refrigerant has been reclaimed; the same owner may reuse it without that step.
notes.source: EPA, Stationary Refrigeration Refrigerant Reclamation Requirements
notes.evidence: restrict the resale of used ozone-depleting and substitute (e.g., HFC) refrigerant to a new owner unless it has been reclaimed by an EPA-certified refrigerant reclaimer. Refrigerant that has been recovered and/or recycled can be returned to the same system or other systems owned by the same person without being reclaimed.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A contractor has recovered refrigerant from one customer’s old system, and a different customer offers to buy it. What must happen first?
notes.back: It must be reclaimed by a certified refrigerant reclaimer.
notes.choices:
A) Reclamation by a certified reclaimer
B) Recycling through filter-driers is enough
C) Nothing, as long as it is the same refrigerant
notes.choicesExplained: B: recycled refrigerant is only for equipment of the same owner. C: the restriction turns on the change of owner, not on the type of refrigerant.
notes.explanation: A sale to a different customer is a change of owner, and the rules restrict resale to a new owner unless the refrigerant has been reclaimed.
notes.source: EPA, Stationary Refrigeration Refrigerant Reclamation Requirements
notes.evidence: restrict the resale of used ozone-depleting and substitute (e.g., HFC) refrigerant to a new owner unless it has been reclaimed by an EPA-certified refrigerant reclaimer.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Where can technicians return recovered refrigerant on its way to reclamation?
notes.back: To a consolidator, such as a refrigerant supplier or recovery company, or in some cases directly to a reclaimer.
notes.explanation: Consolidators package and prepare the refrigerant before reclamation, according to the agency’s page.
notes.source: EPA, Stationary Refrigeration Refrigerant Reclamation Requirements
notes.evidence: Contractors and technicians can return recovered refrigerant to a consolidator (such as a refrigerant manufacturer, supplier, wholesale distributor, or refrigerant recovery company) for packaging and preparation prior to reclamation, or in some cases directly to an EPA reclaimer.

notes.front: Among recovery techniques, the test topics list the need to avoid {{c1::mixing}} refrigerants.
notes.back: mixing
notes.explanation: It is the first item under recovery techniques in the core section of the test topics.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Recovery Techniques”
notes.evidence: Recovery Techniques - Need to avoid mixing refrigerants

notes.front: A technician’s recovery container already holds some R-22, and the next job is an R-134a system. What does the test topics’ recovery guidance point to?
notes.back: Recover the R-134a into a separate container rather than adding it to the R-22.
notes.choices:
A) Use a separate container for the R-134a
B) Add it to the R-22, since both will be reclaimed later
C) Vent the R-22 to make room
notes.choicesExplained: B: the test topics list the need to avoid mixing refrigerants. C: venting refrigerant breaks the Clean Air Act prohibition on venting.
notes.explanation: Adding one refrigerant to a container holding another would mix them, which the test topics list as something recovery must avoid.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Recovery Techniques”
notes.evidence: Recovery Techniques - Need to avoid mixing refrigerants

notes.front: What are two factors the test topics list as affecting the speed of recovery?
notes.back: For example, ambient temperature and hose length. Equipment size and hose diameter are also listed.
notes.explanation: The list ends in “etc.”, so these are examples rather than a complete set.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Recovery Techniques”
notes.evidence: Factors affecting speed of recovery (ambient temperature, size of recycling or recovery equipment, hose length and diameter, etc.)

notes.front: Two recoveries use the same machine on identical units, but one job uses much longer hoses. Which listed speed factor differs between them?
notes.back: Hose length.
notes.explanation: Hose length and diameter are among the factors the test topics say affect the speed of recovery.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Recovery Techniques”
notes.evidence: Factors affecting speed of recovery (ambient temperature, size of recycling or recovery equipment, hose length and diameter, etc.)

notes.front: Two recoveries are the same in every way except that one is done on a hot day and the other on a cold one. Which listed speed factor differs?
notes.back: Ambient temperature.
notes.explanation: Ambient temperature is the first factor the test topics list as affecting the speed of recovery.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Recovery Techniques”
notes.evidence: Factors affecting speed of recovery (ambient temperature, size of recycling or recovery equipment, hose length and diameter, etc.)

notes.front: Two technicians recover from identical units with identical hoses, one using a small recovery machine and one a large machine. Which listed speed factor differs?
notes.back: The size of the recovery equipment.
notes.explanation: The test topics list the size of recycling or recovery equipment among the factors affecting recovery speed.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Recovery Techniques”
notes.evidence: Factors affecting speed of recovery (ambient temperature, size of recycling or recovery equipment, hose length and diameter, etc.)

notes.front: When do the test topics say a system should be evacuated to eliminate air and moisture?
notes.back: At the end of service.
notes.explanation: This is the only item under the dehydration evacuation heading of the core test topics.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Dehydration Evacuation”
notes.evidence: Dehydration Evacuation - Need to evacuate system to eliminate air and moisture at the end of service

notes.front: Repairs are finished on a system that was open to the air. Which step do the test topics list for the end of service?
notes.back: Evacuate the system to eliminate air and moisture: a dehydration evacuation.
notes.choices:
A) Evacuate it to eliminate air and moisture
B) Vent some refrigerant to push the air out
C) Leave it as it is; air does no harm
notes.choicesExplained: B: venting refrigerant breaks the Clean Air Act prohibition on venting. C: the test topics call for eliminating air and moisture at the end of service.
notes.explanation: The test topics call for this evacuation at the end of service, and here the system has taken in air.
notes.source: EPA, Section 608 Technician Certification Test Topics, “Core: Dehydration Evacuation”
notes.evidence: Dehydration Evacuation - Need to evacuate system to eliminate air and moisture at the end of service

notes.front: Under the rule, how must recovery and recycling equipment be used?
notes.back: According to the manufacturer’s directions, unless those directions conflict with the rule’s requirements.
notes.explanation: The rule’s own requirements win where the two disagree; otherwise the directions govern.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F, § 82.156(g)
notes.evidence: (g) All recovery and/or recycling equipment must be used in accordance with the manufacturer's directions unless such directions conflict with the requirements of this subpart.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Who is exempt from having to use certified self-contained recovery equipment?
notes.back: People who service or dispose of only appliances they own that contain pump-out units.
notes.explanation: Both conditions apply: the appliances must be their own, and they must have pump-out units.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F, § 82.156(f)
notes.evidence: (f) Persons who maintain, service, repair, or dispose of only appliances that they own and that contain pump-out units are exempt from the requirement to use certified, self-contained recovery and/or recycling equipment.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Where must certified recovery or recycling equipment have low-loss fittings?
notes.back: On all hoses.
notes.explanation: It is one of the conditions the rule sets for certifying recovery and recycling equipment.
notes.source: 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F, § 82.158(d)(7)
notes.evidence: (7) The equipment must be equipped with low-loss fittings on all hoses.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Before an oil change, to what pressure must the appliance be brought?
notes.back: No higher than 5 psig (pounds per square inch gauge).
notes.explanation: Oil can hold large amounts of dissolved refrigerant, and reducing the pressure first ensures the bulk of it is recovered.
notes.source: EPA, Stationary Refrigeration Service Practice Requirements, “Changing Refrigerant Oil”
notes.evidence: The oil in a refrigeration appliance can contain large amounts of dissolved refrigerant. EPA requires a reduction in the pressure prior to an oil change to ensure that the bulk of the refrigerant contained in the oil is recovered. It is a violation to change oil at higher than 5 psig.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: A technician wants to change the oil in an appliance whose pressure reads 20 psig. What must happen first?
notes.back: Evacuate or pressurise it to no higher than 5 psig; changing oil above that is a violation.
notes.choices:
A) Bring it to no higher than 5 psig
B) Nothing: oil changes have no pressure limit
C) Raise it above 20 psig to push the oil out
notes.choicesExplained: B: the rule makes it a violation to change oil above 5 psig. C: raising the pressure moves the wrong way; the limit is a maximum of 5 psig.
notes.explanation: The rule requires the pressure reduction before any oil change so that the bulk of the refrigerant dissolved in the oil is recovered.
notes.source: EPA, Stationary Refrigeration Service Practice Requirements, “Changing Refrigerant Oil”
notes.evidence: The oil in a refrigeration appliance can contain large amounts of dissolved refrigerant. EPA requires a reduction in the pressure prior to an oil change to ensure that the bulk of the refrigerant contained in the oil is recovered. It is a violation to change oil at higher than 5 psig.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: How do recover, recycle and reclaim differ?
notes.back: Recover: remove and store, untested. Recycle: clean for the same owner’s reuse. Reclaim: reprocess to the purity standard and verify it.
notes.explanation: Recovery needs no testing or processing; recycling does clean the refrigerant, but only for reuse in equipment of the same owner.
notes.source: EPA, Recovering, Recycling, and Reclaiming of Refrigerants
notes.evidence: Recover means to remove refrigerant in any condition from an appliance and to store it in an external container without necessarily testing or processing it in any way - Recycle, when referring to refrigerant, means to extract refrigerant from an appliance (except MVACs) and clean it for reuse in equipment of the same owner
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force

notes.front: Recycled or reclaimed: which refrigerant may be sold to a new owner?
notes.back: Only reclaimed refrigerant, reclaimed by a certified reclaimer. Recycled refrigerant stays with the same owner’s systems.
notes.explanation: The rules restrict resale to a new owner unless the refrigerant has been reclaimed, while recovered or recycled refrigerant may return to the same owner’s systems.
notes.source: EPA, Stationary Refrigeration Refrigerant Reclamation Requirements
notes.evidence: restrict the resale of used ozone-depleting and substitute (e.g., HFC) refrigerant to a new owner unless it has been reclaimed by an EPA-certified refrigerant reclaimer. Refrigerant that has been recovered and/or recycled can be returned to the same system or other systems owned by the same person without being reclaimed.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · 40 CFR Part 82 Subpart F as in force
